_comment: Compiled from Carlisle JB 2012 (Anaesthesia 67:1076-1090) abstract plus the Kranke 2012 'post-Fujii' supplementary note, per compiler/EXTRACTION_SPEC.md. Object-level antiemetic claims only; the Fujii-vs-others contrast is carried by evidence stance + independence_group, not by separate propositions, so 'retract everything in ig_fujii_et_al' is a query over this graph rather than something baked into it.

symbols.label: antiemetic agent
symbols.notes: Type used to bind the unspecified co-administered agent in the synergism and antagonism claims. The abstract never names the partner drug, so it is existentially quantified rather than invented.

symbols.label: postoperative nausea or vomiting
symbols.notes: The composite endpoint the paper reports separately from nausea and from vomiting. Kept distinct because the paper reports distinct effect estimates for it.

symbols.label: rescue antiemesis
symbols.notes: Administration of a rescue antiemetic triggered by postoperative nausea and vomiting.

symbols.label: REDUCES_RISK_OF
symbols.notes: agent lowers the incidence of outcome in population, relative to no prophylaxis / placebo. Used for all monotherapy-efficacy claims.

symbols.label: MORE_EFFECTIVE_THAN
symbols.notes: agent lowers the incidence of outcome more than comparator does. Head-to-head; distinct from REDUCES_RISK_OF because the comparator is an active drug, not placebo.

symbols.label: SYNERGISTIC_WITH
symbols.notes: agent combined with co_agent lowers the incidence of outcome more than agent administered alone.

symbols.label: ANTAGONISTIC_WITH
symbols.notes: agent combined with co_agent lowers the incidence of outcome LESS than agent alone. Deliberately a separate relation and not negate-polarity SYNERGISTIC_WITH: 'no synergism' and 'antagonism' are different claims and the paper asserts both, the first of the combination generally and the second as a further positive finding.

surface_forms: Granisetron was more effective in trials by Fujii et al., relative risk ratios (RRR (95% CI)): nausea 0.53 (0.42-0.67), p=0.00021
if ... articles by Fujii et al. excluded, then the antiemetic effects of granisetron and ramosetron are greatly reduced
Putting the record straight: granisetron's efficacy as an antiemetic 'post-Fujii' ... re-states granisetron's efficacy as a prophylactic antiemetic using only trials not authored by Fujii et al.
propositions.notes: Direction-of-effect claim. The magnitude dispute ('greatly reduced' once Fujii is removed) is deliberately NOT a second proposition: it is the difference between the Fujii and non-Fujii evidence items attached here.

if ... articles by Fujii et al. excluded, then the antiemetic effects of granisetron and ramosetron are greatly reduced

if ... articles by Fujii et al. excluded, then the antiemetic effects of granisetron and ramosetron are greatly reduced
In comparison with granisetron, droperidol was less effective in trials by Fujii et al. than others: nausea 2.41 (1.72-3.36), p=2.5x10(-7)
propositions.notes: Stated in the source as droperidol being inferior to granisetron; encoded as the equivalent granisetron-superiority claim so that it shares a predicate with the other head-to-head claims.

surface_forms: In comparison with granisetron, droperidol was less effective in trials by Fujii et al. than others: ... vomiting 1.73 (1.26-2.38), p=6.4x10(-4)

Triggered rates of rescue were not different in studies by others for droperidol, granisetron and metoclopramide, but were less common after granisetron than droperidol and metoclopramide in studies by Fujii et al., 0.50 (0.38-0.66), p=1.7x10(-6) ... respectively

Triggered rates of rescue were not different in studies by others for droperidol, granisetron and metoclopramide, but were less common after granisetron than droperidol and metoclopramide in studies by Fujii et al., ... 0.47 (0.34-0.64), p=2.6x10(-6), respectively
Postoperative nausea and vomiting was less likely to trigger rescue antiemesis after granisetron and metoclopramide in studies by Fujii et al., 0.40 (0.27-0.60), p=9.7x10(-6)
propositions.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL, flagged. The source reports these two drugs as one pooled analysis, so splitting into a granisetron proposition and a metoclopramide proposition would invent two claims the paper does not separately make; merging them into one would violate 'do not merge claims differing in agent' if read drug-by-drug. Resolved with a disjunctive function term any_of(granisetron, metoclopramide) over the agent role. Also note this estimate is a Fujii-versus-others ratio with no corresponding non-Fujii estimate, so only Fujii evidence is attached: retracting Fujii leaves this UNRESOLVED rather than REFUTED, which is the faithful answer.

surface_forms: in studies by Fujii et al., postoperative nausea and vomiting was more likely if granisetron was administered alone: nausea 4.20 (1.94-9.08), p=2.6x10(-4)
There was no synergism between antiemetics in trials by other authors.
propositions.notes: The source states the contrapositive (PONV more likely on granisetron alone than in combination); that is the synergism claim. The partner drug is never named, hence an existential over antiemetic_agent rather than a fabricated co-agent symbol.

surface_forms: in studies by Fujii et al., postoperative nausea and vomiting was more likely if granisetron was administered alone: ... vomiting 4.50 (2.55-7.97), p=2.3x10(-7)
There was no synergism between antiemetics in trials by other authors.
in studies by Fujii et al., postoperative nausea and vomiting was more likely if granisetron was administered alone: ... nausea or vomiting 5.00 (2.84-8.81), p=2.5x10(-8)
There was no synergism between antiemetics in trials by other authors.
Similarly, droperidol was less effective in studies by Fujii et al. if administered alone: vomiting 2.76 (1.25-6.11), p=0.01
There was no synergism between antiemetics in trials by other authors.
Similarly, droperidol was less effective in studies by Fujii et al. if administered alone: ... nausea or vomiting 2.96 (1.46-6.00), p=2.7x10(-3)
There was no synergism between antiemetics in trials by other authors.
there is no evidence of synergism between antiemetics and indeed, some evidence of antagonism between antiemetic agents
propositions.notes: The only claim in the paper whose sole support is non-Fujii, so it is the one claim that gets STRONGER rather than weaker under a Fujii retraction. Named drugs are not given for the antagonism finding, so both slots are existential. modality=possible because the paper says 'some evidence of', not that antagonism is established.

assertions.notes: Encoded as the original authors asserted it, per spec rule 8, even though Carlisle argues it is an artefact and the underlying articles were later retracted. Retraction is applied by the query, not here.

Supports an attenuated version: 'antiemetic effects ... greatly reduced', i.e. smaller but not abolished. The schema has no strength field on Assertion, so the attenuation lives in this note and in the two opposed-magnitude evidence items.
Carlisle presents the low Fujii rescue rate as an anomaly of the Fujii data rather than a drug property.
Re-states granisetron's prophylactic efficacy using only non-Fujii trials.
